headlines.article_text: Trump denies Musk claim he ordered Starlink restrictions in Ukraine Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points President Trump denied that the White House had ordered restrictions on SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet services in Ukraine this week. Ukrainian officials complained on Tuesday and Wednesday that SpaceX had limited internet connectivity via Starshield without advance notice. Musk said any restrictions on Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine would have come from decisions by the president or White House. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to reporters as he departs the White House on October 16, 2026 in Washington, DC. Andrew Harnik | Getty Images President Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces. Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield , a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government." Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour. Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions." Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX. "Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote . "As your European customers, we are watching you." Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian. The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions. Reuters reported on Thursday , citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order. On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far." Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday. SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. headlines.article_text: Netflix hires Peter Rice to run content. Here's what it means Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Netflix has replaced its chief content officer, Bela Bajaria, with former Disney executive Peter Rice. Rice brings a wealth of experience in television and film, including scripted and unscripted shows, live sports telecasts, prestige television and theatrical distribution. Netflix's viewership has stagnated in recent quarters. It reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday. In this article NFLX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:06 01:06 Netflix’s big executive shakeup: Here’s what you need to know Squawk on the Street Netflix is shaking up its C-suite in an effort to fix its engagement woes. On Thursday, the streaming giant announced that former Disney executive Peter Rice will take over as the company's chief content officer, overseeing global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events. Rice is replacing 10-year Netflix veteran Bela Bajaria , who most recently led the company's global content team with a focus on its live sports strategy . Bajaria was initially hired in 2016 to help the streamer launch an unscripted division as well as licensing and studio co-productions. She later transitioned to the top creative role, spearheading Netflix's $20 billion content budget. She oversaw popular TV series like "Stranger Things," "Wednesday," "Bridgerton," "Squid Game," "Adolescence" and "Beef," as well as Netflix films like "Frankenstein" and "KPop Demon Hunters." Bajaria also helped push Netflix into live sports and events, including deals with the WWE and the NFL as well as programs like "The Roast of Tom Brady." Prior to his stint at Disney, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group as well as Fox's lead executive on the Hulu board. He was also the president of Fox Searchlight Pictures and helped release "Slumdog Millionaire," "Juno," "Little Miss Sunshine" and "Sideways." Peter Rice, seen here on May 3, 2017, was head of Disney's TV entertainment business in 2020. He was one of several executives passed over for the CEO job in favor of Chapek. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images The executive change follows a tumultuous period for Netflix as it faces stagnating viewership and explores avenues for growth. It comes just days after the streaming giant laid off roughly 1,000 employees , or 6% of its workforce. The last time Netflix made cuts of this size was in 2022 when it reported its first quarterly subscriber loss in more than 10 years. "We believe this round of layoffs reflects more structural changes to the cost base than a reaction to near-term subscriber dynamics," wrote Brian Pitz, managing director and head of internet and interactive entertainment equity research at BMO Capital Markets, in a research note published Friday. Flagging engagement In July, Netflix reported viewership increased just 2% in the first half of the year as the streamer suffers from a lack of shows with water-cooler-level hype. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted last month during the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company is "not growing as fast as I want us to." Those warnings, and now Bajaria's exit, have Wall Street bracing for more turbulence ahead. "The sudden departure of Bajaria likely signals to us that user engagement may have remained soft throughout [the third quarter]," Pitz wrote. Netflix is set to release fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday. In July, Nielsen reported that Netflix had generated 7.8% of TV viewership, while YouTube accounted for nearly double that, at 14.2%. YouTube has been Netflix's biggest threat in the battle for viewers' time. In response, the streaming giant has sought to diversify its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention. "If the opportunity is to recast [Netflix] into a broader content hub, the risk is missing the watercooler originals," Steven Cahall, equity analyst at Wells Fargo, wrote in a research note last month. "We see breakout hits as a must for the stock to work again." What Rice brings to Netflix Rice has a wealth of experience in television and film, most recently serving as the chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the company. He managed a wide swath of channels across broadcast and streaming, including ABC, Disney Channel, Hulu and FX Networks. During his tenure, he oversaw the production of more than 300 shows, including "American Idol," "Modern Family," "Abbott Elementary," "The Bear," "Only Murders in the Building" and "Shogun." He also headed up major sporting events such as coverage of the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup. Under Rice's leadership, Disney earned roughly 300 Primetime Emmy nominations between 2021 and 2022. Of those nods, it won nearly 60 awards across its television networks and streaming platforms. Meanwhile, Netflix's Emmy wins have slowed. Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty Images In 2021, it tied the record for most trophies won by an outlet in a single year with 44. This year, however, it only took home 16 prizes, its lowest Emmy haul in a decade. With Rice, Netflix is also getting an executive with theatrical experience. After he was ousted by then-Disney CEO Bob Chapek in mid-2022, he transitioned into an independent producer role. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later." He's currently developing a movie adaptation of the video game "Elden Ring." Late last year, Netflix struck a deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery's film studio and streaming assets, only to be outbid months later by Paramount Skydance, which completed its acquisition of WBD in early October. Some on Wall Street have speculated that the streamer may be interested in further M&A, including acquiring assets from NBCUniversal after it splits from parent company Comcast . "[Rice's] long tenure at Fox, and then Disney after its acquisition of Fox, gives him unique insight into the consolidation of two major studios, relevant if Netflix chooses to go after another studio," Alicia Reese, senior vice president of equity research at Wedbush, wrote in a research note Thursday. "Even if it doesn't, Rice's experience fits well as Netflix pushes deeper into theatrical and builds a broader platform with varied content across the entertainment ecosystem." headlines.article_text: SpaceX policy manger grilled by NYC Council on Grok AI safety, images Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points SpaceX head of global government affairs for AI Gabriela Castillo Madrid faced questions about Grok's generation of sexualized images from the New York City Council on Friday. NYC Council Speaker Julie Menin asked why she was able to pull up sexualized images of herself when Castillo Madrid said Grok does not let users create such images of real people. Elon Musk's aerospace and AI company previously evaded a subpoena to testify as part of a legislative investigation and hearing held last week. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The SpaceX headquarters is seen on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026 in Hawthorne, CA. Eric Thayer | Los Angeles Times | Getty Images SpaceX artificial intelligence policy leader Gabriela Castillo Madrid faced a tough line of questioning from NYC Council Speaker Julie Menin and other members on Friday as part of a council investigation into AI safety. When Castillo Madrid claimed that the company had appropriate "safeguards" in place around its AI products, Menin immediately confronted her. "I'm going to completely push back on that," Menin said. "I mean, just this morning — myself and my team — we put our own names, my own name, into Grok, and there's absolutely a sexualized image of myself. So then, how is it that within a second, I could find a sexualized image of myself using Grok?" Castillo Madrid responded that the company has "strict controls" and would have the safety team look into that specific instance. NYC Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, who leads the council's tech committee, told Castillo Madrid that "it is disgusting" that Grok enables users to easily "sexualize" images of real women without their consent. "I just don't understand how you can say that there are these safe models," Menin said. "It's just unacceptable." Castillo Madrid appeared in front of the council's tech committee by video. Elon Musk's aerospace, defense tech and AI company originally evaded requests and a subpoena from the city council to appear alongside leaders from OpenAI , Anthropic , Google and Meta on Oct. 5. SpaceX agreed to testify earlier this week after the council threatened to have its subpoena enforced by a judge. The council opened its probe following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models, and is aiming to use testimony and information unearthed through the investigation to guide new regulations. Read more CNBC tech news Amazon launches new Bee 'personal AI' devices that listen to conversations Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urges U.S.-China dialogue on 'potentially dangerous' AI OpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concerns Anthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPO Before Castillo Madrid took a role in government affairs at SpaceX earlier this year, she worked at X, Musk's social media company that's now owned by SpaceX, according to her LinkedIn profile . Prior to that, she spent almost three years at the U.S. Department of Commerce. De La Rosa asked Castillo Madrid how many whistleblowers the company has fired, to which Castillo Madrid said she was "not aware" of any. "I just want to interject for a minute because Devin Kim, one of your former employees, was reportedly fired after he sounded the alarm about serious safety concerns," Menin said. "I'm not aware with that specific case," Castillo Madrid responded, adding that the company has a culture where "everybody has a an ability to say something when they see something." Kim is now President of the nonprofit Center for AI Safety, a think tank focused on AI risks and safety. Kim began his testimony before the council by outlining his experience as one of the first employees at xAI, saying that he "built the systems that researchers use to train and evaluate Grok." Kim said that he started raising concerns in January 2025 and those worries were shut down by his manager. "My supervisor responded that AI safety was useless, and that AI would kill us and all anyways," he said. Kim appeared by video, along with his attorney, following Castillo Madrid's questioning. Regarding Grok-generated images, Kim said under prior standards at the company, "tasteful nudity was acceptable and is the goal." "During my time there, there were only three employees working on AI safety, many of whom left after I resigned," Kim said. "And I think in large part due to the frustration with how safety was being handled." The council also pressed Castillo Madrid about other areas of misuse with Grok and the types of safeguards that were in place. Councilmember Mercedes Narcisse asked why the company promoted the idea of users uploading X-rays to Grok, asking if that was safe and if HIPPA protections applied. SpaceX's Castillo Madrid said Grok is "not meant to be a clinician, a doctor," adding, "in terms of privacy, users decide whether their Grok conversations are used to train our models or not." Narcisse said it was dangerous to tell people "openly on X, to put their MRI, X-rays," into Grok and expect "a definite answer" on health matters. The council member then upbraided the SpaceX representative for the vagueness of some of her replies. "You're supposed to give us answers. You're not," she said. In merging SpaceX with xAI in February, Musk combined his AI and social networking business with his rocket launch company, which also owns the Starlink satellite internet service. The merger put SpaceX in control of AI model Grok, which is used by some federal agencies, including the Pentagon . SpaceX went public in June and is now valued at about $2 trillion. In August, SpaceX completed a $60 billion acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor. In skipping the earlier NYC Council hearing, SpaceX avoided direct questioning from a member of the U.K. Parliament, Jess Asato, who testified about experiencing AI-enabled online harassment. Asato is suing xAI in the U.K. after Grok users created and distributed sexualized images of her online without her consent. She's seeking damages, alleging misuse of her private information and breaches of European data protection rules. According to the BBC , Asato criticized SpaceX for its "arrogance" in not appearing last week. SpaceX didn't respond to a request for comment ahead of the meeting. headlines.article_text: Stock market today: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading on Oct. 14, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago | Getty Images Stocks slid on Friday as traders headed for a mostly losing week amid a shift away from tech and artificial intelligence-related names as well as a rise in oil prices. The S&P 500 traded down 1.2%, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 2.3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average outperformed as it fell 275 points, or 0.5%. Chipmakers were lower again. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) lost 1%, led by declines in Micron Technology , Advanced Micro Devices and Sandisk . Semiconductors have struggled this week amid jitters about competition from China . The SMH is down 8% week to date, on pace for its biggest weekly decline since July. Those declines, coupled with drops in other stocks linked to AI, put the S&P 500 on pace for a losing week. The benchmark index is down more than 2% this week, while the Nasdaq has shed more than 4%. The tech-heavy index was on track for its worst week since June. The Dow, on the other hand, has moved higher by less than 1% on the week. Investors have also grown concerned that tech companies are borrowing too much for the AI buildout . Shares of neoclouds like CoreWeave , which has seen its total debt rise to more than $51 billion , were down 10%, putting the stock's week-to-date losses at more than 23%. "The question is: Is this a systemic issue?" said Michael Rosen, Angeles' chief investment officer. "Obviously, increased debt issuance is something to observe and continue to watch and be concerned about if it continues to get to levels of excessiveness. But we're not remotely close to that right now." Other areas of the market such as energy saw gains Friday, with stocks like Chevron helping to keep the Dow's losses in check. That's as oil prices moved higher amid rising tensions between the U.S. and Iran as well as between Russian and Ukraine. West Texas Intermediate crude futures increased 3.51% to settle at $101.41 per barrel, while Brent crude futures advanced 3.72% to $109.86. Simultaneously, investors have been grappling with hotter-than-expected inflation data, which has been exacerbated by elevated energy prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war. Wholesale inflation this week saw its biggest gain since 2022 , while consumer inflation remained well above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke at an IMF event in Bangkok overnight. And while he didn't comment on whether the Fed would raise rates before year-end, traders took that as a sign that the central bank will hold policy steady later this month. The CME Group's FedWatch tool points to an 85% chance the Fed keeps its overnight rate unchanged at its Oct. 27-28 meeting. 12 Min Ago Volatility index rises to highest level since June As the market sell-off intensified Friday afternoon, the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) rose to levels it last closed at four months ago. The VIX rose to 21.32, as of 3:10 p.m., rising more than 4.8 points on the session. It's on pace for its highest close since June 10, when it closed at 22.22. Typically, when the VIX is above 20 that indicates greater fear in the market. The index last closed above that level on July 29 , when markets fell after the Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady at its meeting that month. The next day , stocks rose, and the day marked a bottom in a market where many AI-related stocks had been selling off in the previous month . The two sectors were down 2.7% and 2.4%, respectively, becoming the two biggest laggards among the 11 S&P 500 sectors. Consumer discretionary followed behind them, falling 1.5%. However, a look beneath the surface showed that the S&P 500 — which was last down 1.3% — was more evenly split despite the losses at the index level. There were about 280 losers in the index and 222 gainers. In total, five out of the 11 S&P 500 sectors were in positive territory, led by energy with its 2.1% gain and utilities with its rise of 1.2%. — Sean Conlon and Sarah Min 2 Hours Ago U.S. crude oil surpasses $100 In an aerial view, oil storage tanks are seen at the rail-fed diesel base, Exxon/Mobil Wink Transloading facility on Aug. 13, 2026 in Wink, Texas. Independent Bank earned $1.90 per share, topping the FactSet consensus call for $1.85 per share. Net interest income of $220.7 million also beat the $218.5 million estimate. The bank sees home equity loans growing by a high single-digit annualized percentage in the fourth quarter. Moog — The manufacturer of precision motor control systems rose more than 4%. In recent months, that bet has paid off for the value investor. After falling about 40% in the first quarter of 2026, during which the enterprise software stock at various points was trading at not even three times revenue, the stock went on to surge more than 55% in the third. It's also outperforming this week, rising more than 2% amid a broader tech sell-off as investors exit for safer assets.
